ai.title: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is a disorder where antibodies destroy red cells, causing anemia, jaundice and possible life‑threatening complications. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical clues and targeted laboratory tests, many of which may be limited in low‑resource settings.

b: Warm IgG‑mediated AIHA (most common) – active at 37 °C
Cold IgM‑mediated (cold agglutinin disease) – active below 30 °C
sections.p: AIHA occurs when the immune system produces antibodies that bind to red blood cells (RBCs) and trigger their premature destruction. The disease can be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to infections, drugs, malignancy or systemic autoimmune disease.

b: Reticulocyte count rises >2 % as marrow compensates
LDH elevated, haptoglobin low or undetectable
Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) positive for IgG and/or C3
sections.p: The hemolysis is intravascular (complement‑mediated) or extravascular (splenic macrophage clearance). The resulting anemia, reticulocytosis and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia produce the classic clinical picture.

b: Consider recent malaria treatment, quinine‑related AIHA
HIV infection can cause warm AIHA via polyclonal activation
TB and hepatitis B may be associated with secondary AIHA
sections.p: Patients present with fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine and splenomegaly. In low‑resource hospitals, malaria, HIV and TB can mimic or trigger hemolysis, so a careful history is essential.

t.b: Shows spherocytes or agglutination → supports hemolysis; if unavailable, rely on CBC trends
Answers whether antibodies/complement are bound to RBCs; positive DAT confirms immune hemolysis
Answers the degree of hemolysis; high indirect bilirubin, high LDH, low haptoglobin indicate active destruction

t.a: Cold agglutinin titre (if cold AIHA suspected)
t.b: Answers presence of IgM cold antibodies; titre ≥1:64 at 4 °C is significant

b: Distinguish warm AIHA (IgG, splenomegaly) from cold agglutinin disease (IgM, acrocyanosis)
Know that steroids are first‑line for warm AIHA; avoid splenectomy in active infection
sections.p: Examiners often test your ability to differentiate AIHA from other causes of anemia and to outline immediate management steps.

b: If steroids fail: Rituximab (if available) or azathioprine – target B‑cells
Cold AIHA: Keep patient warm, avoid cold exposure, consider rituximab
Transfusion: Use least‑incompatible, washed RBCs; give only if life‑threatening anemia
sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger, suppress the immune response, and provide supportive care. In low‑resource settings, prioritize readily available drugs and transfusion safety.

b: Malaria‑induced hemolysis – peripheral smear shows parasites
G6PD deficiency – triggers hemolysis after oxidative stress, DAT negative
Sickle cell crisis – sickled cells on smear, hemoglobin electrophoresis diagnostic
sections.p: Conditions that also cause anemia and jaundice can be mistaken for AIHA.

b: Haptoglobin may be normal early in hemolysis; rely on LDH and bilirubin
DAT can be negative in low‑titer antibodies; repeat if suspicion high
sections.p: Certain lab values may be falsely normal, especially when tests are limited.
